name: Sentaa-guy

lead: Sentaa guy (Center Guy) is a Japanese youth fashion subculture from Shibuya, Tokyo, described as the male equivalent of the yamanba or manba look. The name puns on Center Gai, the pedestrian shopping street near Shibuya Station. It grew out of gyaru-o, men who dressed in styles meant to suit gyaru culture.

The appeal is bold, high-contrast presentation: very dark tan, wolf cuts with extensions in bright colours, highlighter and white lip concealer, and decorative details. It is documented through fashion-history pages rather than research.

paras: Followers built the look from a deep tan, a wolf cut with extensions and dramatic crown volume in white, blonde, pink or primary colours, manba-like makeup with coloured contact lenses, and tropical-print clothing. They gathered around Center Gai, danced to trance, and used their own slang.

Tanning exposes the skin to ultraviolet radiation, and repeated bleaching can damage hair. Socially, some businesses restricted the group: ALBA ROSA stores reportedly barred them from trying on clothes, and the Shibuya nightclub atom banned Center Guys and manba.

chain: Very deep tan and bright, voluminous hair
High-contrast, recognisable look within the Shibuya scene
angle.text: Adopters change skin tone, hair colour and makeup to create a bold, recognisable look that signals membership of the Center Gai scene. The effect is visual and stylistic rather than a change in underlying features.

lead: Sentaa guy (センターガイ, "Center Guy") is a Japanese male street-fashion style associated with Shibuya, Tokyo, described as the male equivalent of the yamanba look. The name is a pun on Center Gai, the pedestrian shopping street near Shibuya Station.[1]

The style grew out of gyaru-o, men who adopted fashions designed to appeal to gyaru women. Center Guy is described as emerging around 2003 as a distinct substyle on Center Street, and the magazine Men's egg feature "Hello! Center GUY" and a 2004 SMAP×SMAP television parody skit are credited with boosting its popularity.[2]

The look mirrors ganguro and manba for women: a tan that reached the darkest shades, voluminous brightly coloured hair, and flashy makeup.[1][2] For people interested in appearance, it is an example of an exaggerated, high-contrast style in which skin tone, hair colour and makeup are used deliberately as statements.

paras: Ganguro, a women's style peaking around 2000, combined a deep tan with red, blonde or silver-grey hair, and yamanba or manba was a more extreme offshoot with white lipstick, pastel eye makeup and glittery adhesives.[1] Sentaa guy is listed as the male equivalent, with the same pun-based naming on Shibuya's Center Gai street.[1]

Galture's account describes tans darker than typical gyaru-o, reaching the darkest ganguro shades. Hair was cut as a wolf cut with extensions, with dramatic crown volume in white, blonde, pink or primary colours, which the page compares to the look of the anime character Super Saiyan. Makeup resembled manba makeup, with coloured contacts, highlighter on the nose bridge and around the eyes, and white concealer on the lips. They favoured the hibiscus-print brand ALBA ROSA and its men's line MY TANE.[2]

Center Guys were described as outgoing, using their own slang called "GUY language" and forming groups through mutual recognition. They loved trance music and danced para-para in Shibuya, with hangouts including a photo-booth spot and the Center Street McDonald's.[2]

Reception was mixed: ALBA ROSA stores reportedly barred them from trying on clothes, and the nightclub atom banned both Center Guys and manba. The community later dwindled and the look disappeared from the streets.[2]

timeline.event: Ganguro emerges in Shibuya and Ikebukuro, peaking around 2000.[1]
Center Guy emerges on Center Street as a gyaru-o substyle.[2]
A SMAP×SMAP skit parodying Center Guys boosts the look's popularity.[2]
